block.comment: The lookbehind mirrors the compiler's own scanner, which requires whitespace before the name. This pattern is only the BARE attribute form, where the name and the `=` are coloured too; a block in expression position is `ramonda.css-value`. The `@@` is this language's MARKER and is coloured as one wherever it appears. It opens a BLOCK and nothing else does: `if ({ … })` and `...{ … }` carry no sigil, because inside a block the language is the block's own. A user reported the two characters coming out as punctuation in one place and a keyword in another, which is a reader having to learn that the same marker means two things. The BRACKET keeps `punctuation.section.embedded.begin`, and that is not cosmetic: it is what pairs with the `contentName` an editor reads to treat the inside as CSS.

innards.comment: Order is the whole of it. A hole is ONE brace, and so is a nested rule's body — so every pattern that can recognise a hole from its POSITION runs before `#nested`, which would otherwise read `color: ` as a selector and the hole as a rule list. Measured: it did exactly that, and the CSS grammar agreed with it, scoping `accent` as a property name.

nested.comment: A nested rule. The editor's CSS grammar has no pattern for one — measured, `&:hover {` comes back as a property whose value is `hover {` — so the block handles nesting itself. It runs LAST among the brace patterns: everything that can tell a hole by its position has already had the line, so a `{` reaching here opens a rule.

patterns.comment: `&` is CSS nesting's own, and the editor's CSS grammar has no pattern for it either.
patterns.name: entity.other.attribute-name.parent-selector.css

composition.comment: This language's own markers, which CSS has no idea about — measured, the CSS grammar read `if (` as a selector and `...` as nothing at all. Each one CONSUMES its hole rather than only colouring the marker: with one brace the hole left behind would be read as a rule body.

patterns.comment: `if ({ … })` opens a conditional group. Measured in Chromium 151: `if (x) { … }` in a prelude is DROPPED, because a type selector may not be followed by parentheses and a functional pseudo-class needs its colon — and nothing in CSS starts with a bare word and takes parens. The `(` is what makes it unambiguous, and it is why the condition needs no position rule of its own: a `(` is not a place a rule can open. `if` carried a `@@` until 2026-09-10; the sigil opens a BLOCK now and nothing else does.
`...{ … };` merges another block's map here, in the position a declaration would be.

hole-in-a-name.comment: A hole standing in a property NAME — `{accent}: #34d399`, the only way to set a registered property. Recognised by what FOLLOWS it: a brace pair with a colon after it. A rule's body cannot look like that, because nothing follows its `}` but the next item. The leading `\s*` is there for the same reason as in `#declaration-with-a-hole`: to start where `#nested` starts, so order decides between them rather than indentation.

declaration-with-a-hole.comment:
A declaration whose value holds a hole, matched whole so the CSS grammar never sees the `{`.

The lookahead is the discriminator the parser uses, written as a regex: a property name, a colon, and then WHITESPACE OR THE BRACE ITSELF — and a `{` before any `;` or `}`. The space is load-bearing and a probe found it: `a:hover { … }` is a legal prelude and begins with a property-shaped name and a colon exactly like `border: 4px solid` does. A declaration's colon is followed by whitespace or its value; a pseudo-class's is followed at once by its own name.

A declaration with no hole is left to the CSS grammar, so nothing that worked stops working.

The leading `\s*` is not decoration. TextMate picks the pattern whose match starts EARLIEST in the line, and `#nested` begins with `[^;{}]+?`, which happily starts at the indentation — so a pattern anchored at the property name always lost to it. Measured: the rule won, and the CSS grammar then scoped the hole's expression as a property name.

patterns.comment: The hole itself. Inside a value there is nothing else a `{` can be.
